The petitioner (appellant herein) had preferred a suit under Section 13(1)(1-a) (1-b) of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955 in which it has been stated that the marriage of the petitioner was solemnized with the respondent (respondent herein also) on 02.05.2008 as per Hindu rites and customs and out of the said wedlock, the respondent had given birth to twins, both girls in July 2011.
On account of the pressure created by the respondent, the petitioner was compelled to rent a separate accommodation at Madhupur at a distance of 25 kms. from his house.

It has been stated that while living in Bhalgarha, the respondent always used to quarrel and threaten the petitioner, his mother,
brothers and sister of implicating them in false criminal cases and also pressurized the petitioner to hand over his entire salary to her.
The respondent did not involve herself in domestic chores and did not even cook for the petitioner and his mother.
During the one and half year stay at Madhupur, the respondent always threatened the petitioner of dire consequences if the entire salary is not handed over to her and also humiliated and slapped him.

It has been stated that the respondent was taken to the house of her father in February 2011 by the father of the respondent when she was pregnant and when the petitioner visited the respondent, she always behaved rudely and humiliated the petitioner.
Even after the birth of twin daughters, the respondent refused to come back to her matrimonial house and agreed to return back if the entire salary is handed over to her.
The respondent has deserted the petitioner from the month of February 2012 and did not allow the petitioner to establish physical relationship with her.

It has been stated that the petitioner, despite being subjected to mental torture, requested the respondent to accompany her and being constrained, the petitioner had filed an application for restitution of conjugal rights under Section 9 of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955.
Immediately on receipt of the notice, the respondent had filed a case under Section 498A IPC and Section 3/4 of Dowry Prohibition Act against the petitioner and his family members.

The petitioner had filed an application for anticipatory bail which was rejected on 30.09.2013 against which the petitioner had preferred ABA No. 4554 of 2013 before the Jharkhand High Court which was allowed on the condition that the petitioner will keep the respondent with him with full dignity and honour.

In spite of the written undertaking given by the petitioner, the respondent refused to accompany the petitioner and repeated the same terms and conditions which she was insisting upon since the beginning.
The petitioner was appointed as a teacher on compassionate ground on account of the death of his father and he was duty bound to maintain the dependents of his father.
Since the respondent had refused to accompany the petitioner, he was compelled to file an application on 03-03-2014 informing about such refusal.
The respondent had filed an application for cancellation of the bail granted to the petitioner in which a rejoinder was filed by the petitioner.

It has been stated that the respondent has continuously committed mental torture upon the petitioner by her various acts and has also deserted the petitioner and on these twin grounds the suit was filed seeking dissolution of marriage.
5. The respondent on being noticed had appeared and filed a written statement in which the allegation leveled against her has been denied.

7. The petitioner has examined two witnesses in support of his case.
8. P.W.1 Dilip Kumar Jha is the petitioner who has stated about solemnization of his marriage with the respondent on 02.05.2008 as per Hindu rites and customs.
On account of the death of his father, he was provided with compassionate appointment subject to the condition that he is to look after his aged mother.

After one month of the marriage, the respondent without any reason started quarrelling with his mother and two younger brothers as a result of which he had to take a house on rent at Madhupur which was 25 kilometers from his house.

The respondent while staying at the rented house started putting pressure upon him to hand over the entire salary to her and make the expenses as per her dictates in order to prevent him to give any financial assistance to his aged mother.
This led to constant fights and the respondent used to regularly assault him.
He tolerated such behaviour and in the meantime the respondent became pregnant as a result of which his father-in-law took the respondent to his house in February 2011.
Whenever he went to his in-law's place at Sarath to give some money, the respondent and her father used to abuse him and pressurise him to part with his salary.
In July 2011, twins were born to the respondent and he had given Rs 15,000/- towards the expenses of delivery but he was abused and publicly humiliated.

Since the respondent was not inclined to come to her matrimonial house despite the efforts made by him, he had filed a suit under Section 9 of the Hindu Marriage Act for restitution of conjugal rights and in the said suit after notice was received by the respondent, she had filed a false criminal case being Karon P.S. Case No. 61/2013.
His younger brother Subodh Kumar Jha had to go to jail due to the lodging of the said case.
After he was granted bail by the High Court, he had tried his best to bring back the respondent and the children but the respondent refused to go with him.
The respondent had instead filed an application for cancellation of the bail granted to him.

13. It has been submitted by Ms. Saman Ahmad, learned counsel for the petitioner/appellant that the petitioner has been able to show several instances which would indicate about the torture committed upon the petitioner by the respondent.

The petitioner was forced to leave his own house as well as his old- aged mother, brothers and sister on account of the incessant pressure created upon him by the respondent and he had to take a rented house at Madhupur far off from his own house.

It has come in course of evidence that there was too much interference on the part of the father of the respondent in the marital life of the petitioner and constant demand was made to hand over the entire salary of the petitioner to the respondent.

The respondent had extended her act of cruelty to the mother of the petitioner also and so long as she was at her matrimonial house, she neither did any domestic chores nor did she cook food and left the mother of the petitioner to fend for herself.

It has been submitted that the respondent has forsaken all her duties and obligations towards the petitioner and there has been a willful abandonment on her part and the marriage has become dead for all practical purposes.
Though the petitioner has been able to prove cruelty as well as desertion, the learned trial court has not appreciated the evidence of the petitioner and the other circumstances.

14. Mr. Pran Pranay, learned counsel appearing for the respondent/wife has submitted that the taking of a rented house by the petitioner at Madhupur was not due to the reason as enunciated by the petitioner, but on account of his oblique motive to grab an amount of Rs.1,75,000/- from the father of the respondent in order to purchase a plot of land.

The petitioner had never visited the respondent even on the birth of the twin daughters nor did he make any attempt to bring the respondent back to his home despite an undertaking given before the court and this would clearly show that it was the petitioner who had deserted the respondent and not the other way round as projected by the petitioner.

Due to the torture committed upon the respondent, she had instituted a case under Section 498A IPC against the petitioner and his family members which itself is a cause to stay separate, though the respondent in her evidence has clearly stated about her willingness to resume her marital life with the petitioner provided she is kept with honour and dignity.
15. We have heard the learned counsel for the respective sides and have also perused the trial court records.

'Cruelty' has not been defined in the Hindu Marriage Act 1955, though the spectrum of cruelty has broadened with the course of time by virtue of the various judgments of the Hon'ble Supreme Court.

In the case of Shobha Rani v. Madhukar Reddi reported in (1988) 1 SCC 105 it has been held as follows:-
"4. Section 13(1)(i-a) uses the words "treated the petitioner with cruelty".

entities.text: Shobha Rani v. Madhukar Reddi reported in (1988) 1 SCC 105
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: The word "cruelty" has not been defined.
Indeed it could not have been defined.
It has been used in relation to human conduct or human behaviour.
It is the conduct in relation to or in respect of matrimonial duties and obligations.
It is a course of conduct of one which is adversely affecting the other.

The cruelty may be mental or physical,
intentional or unintentional.
If it is physical the court will have no problem to determine it.
It is a question of fact and degree.
If it is mental the problem presents difficulty.
First, the enquiry must begin as to the nature of the cruel treatment.
Second, the impact of such treatment on the mind of the spouse.
Whether it caused reasonable apprehension that it would be harmful or injurious to live with the other.
Ultimately, it is a matter of inference to be drawn by taking into account the nature of the conduct and its effect on the complaining spouse.
There may, however, be cases where the conduct complained of itself is bad enough and per se unlawful or illegal.
Then the impact or the injurious effect on the other spouse need not be enquired into or considered.

In such cases, the cruelty will be established if the conduct itself is proved or admitted."
17.

'Cruelty' has also been considered in the case of A. Jayachandra v. Aneel Kaur reported in (2005)
2 SCC 22 where it has been held as follows:-

entities.text:
A. Jayachandra v. Aneel Kaur reported in (2005)
2 SCC 22
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: "10. The expression "cruelty" has not been defined in the Act.
Cruelty can be physical or mental.

Cruelty which is a ground for dissolution of marriage may be defined as wilful and unjustifiable conduct of such character as to cause danger to life, limb or health, bodily or mental, or as to give rise to a reasonable apprehension of such a danger.

The question of mental cruelty has to be considered in the light of the norms of marital ties of the particular society to which the parties belong, their social values,
status, environment in which they live.
Cruelty, as noted above, includes mental cruelty, which falls within the purview of a matrimonial wrong.
Cruelty need not be physical.

If from the conduct of the spouse same is established and/or an inference can be legitimately drawn that the treatment of the spouse is such that it causes an apprehension in the mind of the other spouse, about his or her mental welfare then this conduct amounts to cruelty.

In a delicate human relationship like matrimony,
one has to see the probabilities of the case.

The concept, proof beyond the shadow of doubt, is to be applied to criminal trials and not to civil matters and certainly not to matters of such delicate personal relationship as those of husband and wife.

Therefore, one has to see what are the probabilities in a case and legal cruelty has to be found out, not merely as a matter of fact, but as the effect on the mind of the complainant spouse because of the acts or omissions of the other.
Cruelty may be physical or corporeal or may be mental.
In physical cruelty, there can be tangible and direct evidence, but in the case of mental cruelty there may not at the same time be direct evidence.

6 probe into the mental process and mental effect of incidents that are brought out in evidence.

sentences.text: It is in this view that one has to consider the evidence in matrimonial disputes.
11. The expression "cruelty" has been used in relation to human conduct or human behaviour.
It is the conduct in relation to or in respect of matrimonial duties and obligations.
Cruelty is a course or conduct of one, which is adversely affecting the other.
The cruelty may be mental or physical, intentional or unintentional.
If it is physical, the court will have no problem in determining it.
It is a question of fact and degree.
If it is mental, the problem presents difficulties.

First, the enquiry must begin as to the nature of cruel treatment, second the impact of such treatment in the mind of the spouse, whether it caused reasonable apprehension that it would be harmful or injurious to live with the other.
Ultimately, it is a matter of inference to be drawn by taking into account the nature of the conduct and its effect on the complaining spouse.
However, there may be a case where the conduct complained of itself is bad enough and per se unlawful or illegal.
Then the impact or injurious effect on the other spouse need not be enquired into or considered.
In such cases, the cruelty will be established if the conduct itself is proved or admitted.

(See Shobha Rani v. Madhukar Reddi.)
12.
To constitute cruelty, the conduct complained of should be "grave and weighty" so as to come to the conclusion that the petitioner spouse cannot be reasonably expected to live with the other spouse.
It must be something more serious than "ordinary wear and tear of married life".
The conduct, taking into consideration the circumstances and background has to be examined to reach the conclusion whether the conduct complained of amounts to cruelty in the matrimonial law.
Conduct has to be considered, as noted above, in the background of several factors such as social status of parties, their education, physical and mental conditions, customs and traditions.
It is difficult to lay down a precise definition or to give exhaustive description of the circumstances, which would constitute cruelty.

It must be of the type as to satisfy the conscience of the court that the relationship between the parties had deteriorated to such an extent due to the conduct of the other spouse that it would be impossible for them to live together without mental agony, torture or distress, to entitle the complaining spouse to secure divorce.

Physical violence is not absolutely essential to constitute cruelty and a consistent course of conduct inflicting immeasurable mental agony and torture may well constitute cruelty within the meaning of Section 10 of the Act.

Mental cruelty may consist of verbal abuses and insults by using filthy and abusive language leading to constant disturbance of mental peace of the other party."

sentences.text: The respondent was taken to her parental house by her father where she became pregnant and after the birth of the twins the petitioner had made several efforts to bring her back including filing of a suit for restitution of conjugal rights but the respondent refused which has been construed by the petitioner to be an act of willful abandonment.

19. The respondent, on the other hand, has denied such insinuation and has reflected on the torture committed upon her for which she had to take recourse to instituting a criminal case which ended in a compromise but the petitioner even then had not taken her back to her matrimonial house.
The petitioner has not visited the paternal house of the respondent even after the birth of the children nor had he extended any financial assistance to the respondent.

20. The petitioner has stated that an acrimonious relationship existed between him and the respondent on account of the various acts of the respondent demanding the entire salary of the petitioner and restricting the expenses incurred by the petitioner to prevent the petitioner from giving any amount to his mother and these acts at Madhupur where both stayed in a rented house seems to have been falsified by the fact that the respondent conceived while staying in the same house which indicates that the relationship between them was not volatile as has been made out by the petitioner.

21. The respondent had filed a criminal case against the petitioner and his family members and charge sheet has been submitted against the petitioner and his brothers and sister as per the evidence of the witnesses and since the said case has not reached its logical conclusion, it can be inferred that the respondent was tortured and ousted by the petitioner from his house.
The petitioner has been unable to prove cruelty; rather it seems that it was the respondent who was at the receiving end of the cruelty and torture meted out by the petitioner.

The petitioner (P.W.1) in his cross-examination has admitted that save and accept an amount of Rs. 20,000/- given to the respondent at the time of child birth which has been denied by the respondent, he has not extended any financial assistance which to a great extent supports the assertion of the respondent (R.W.1)

sentences.text: We have given careful consideration to her submissions.
Firstly, we deal with the issue of desertion.
The learned counsel appearing for the appellant relied upon the decision of this Court in Lachman Utamchand Kirpalani which has been consistently followed in several decisions of this Court.
The law consistently laid down by this Court is that desertion means the intentional abandonment of one spouse by the other without the consent of the other and without a reasonable cause.

The deserted Dilip Kumar Jha Son Of Late Paresh ... vs Seema Kumari Jha Wife Of Dilip Kumar Jha on 3 November, 2025 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/163329952/

sentences.text: spouse must prove that there is a factum of separation and there is an intention on the part of deserting spouse to bring the cohabitation to a permanent end.
In other words, there should be animus deserendi on the part of the deserting spouse.
There must be an absence of consent on the part of the deserted spouse and the conduct of the deserted spouse should not give a reasonable cause to the deserting spouse to leave the matrimonial home.
The view taken by this Court has been incorporated in the Explanation added to sub-section (1) of Section 13 by Act 68 of 1976.

The said Explanation reads thus:
"13. Divorce.--(1) * * * Explanation.--In this sub-section, the expression "desertion"
means the desertion of the petitioner by the other party to the marriage without reasonable cause and without the consent or against the wish of such party, and includes the wilful neglect of the petitioner by the other party to the marriage, and its grammatical variations and cognate expressions shall be construed accordingly."
23.
The 'intentional' abandonment without any reasonable cause as harped by the learned counsel for the petitioner is totally absent in the present case.

The respondent has given out a justifiable reason for her stay at her parental house coupled with the conduct of the petitioner and his stream of discontentment and disenchantment with the respondent has cascaded down to his children also which can be deciphered from his cross-examination and which we have noticed above.

The respondent has expressed her willingness to resume her marital life with the petitioner but the petitioner has not showed his inclination to keep the respondent with him with full dignity and honour.
The facts of the case in no circumstances can be said to constitute desertion and Issue No.(iv) has also been correctly answered against the respondent.

24. We therefore on the basis of the discussions made herein above do not find any reason to interfere in the impugned judgment dated 16.05.2018 passed by Shri Nikesh Kumar Sinha, learned Principal Judge, Family Court, Deoghar in Matrimonial (Divorce) Suit No. 187 of 2014 and consequently this appeal is dismissed.
25. Pending Interlocutory application, if any, stands closed.

Therefore, one has to see what are the probabilities in a case and legal cruelty has to be found out, not merely as a matter of fact, but as the effect on the mind of the complainant spouse because of the acts or omissions of the other.
Cruelty may be physical or corporeal or may be mental.
In physical cruelty, there can be tangible and direct evidence, but in the case of mental cruelty there may not at the same time be direct evidence.
It is the conduct in relation to or in respect of matrimonial duties and obligations.
Cruelty is a course or conduct of one, which is adversely affecting the other.
The cruelty may be mental or physical, intentional or unintentional.
It is a question of fact and degree.
Ultimately, it is a matter of inference to be drawn by taking into account the nature of the conduct and its effect on the complaining spouse.
However, there may be a case where the conduct complained of itself is bad enough and per se unlawful or illegal.
Then the impact or injurious effect on the other spouse need not be enquired into or considered.
In such cases, the cruelty will be established if the conduct itself is proved or admitted.
(See Shobha Rani v. Madhukar Reddi.)
12.
To constitute cruelty, the conduct complained of should be "grave and weighty" so as to come to the conclusion that the petitioner spouse cannot be reasonably expected to live with the other spouse.
It must be something more serious than "ordinary wear and tear of married life".
The conduct, taking into consideration the circumstances and background has to be examined to reach the conclusion whether the conduct complained of amounts to cruelty in the matrimonial law.

In other words, there should be animus deserendi on the part of the deserting spouse.
There must be an absence of consent on the part of the deserted spouse and the conduct of the deserted spouse should not give a reasonable cause to the deserting spouse to leave the matrimonial home.
The facts of the case in no circumstances can be said to constitute desertion and Issue No.(iv) has also been correctly answered against the respondent.
